It took a while for scholars to trace the domestication of cats. Because the skeletons of wild and domesticated cats are so similar, archeological evidence can be hard to decipher. Some of the earliest evidence of cat domestication comes from Cyprus. Archeologists found the skeleton of a cat buried by a human, indicating that the feline was a pet. Scholars think that cat domestication began 10,000 to 12,000 years ago. This time frame coincides with when the first farming societies flourished in the Fertile Crescent. When humans were hunter-gatherers, dogs were of great use as hunting aides and thus were domesticated much earlier than cats. Cats became useful when humans settled and began growing crops and storing food. With food storage came mice. Cats and humans shared a helpful relationship, as prey was ample for felines, and humans had pest control.

The domestic cat originated from Felis silvestris lybica. The family Felidae arose about 10 to 11 million years ago. Most domesticated animals are pack or herd animals with clear hierarchical structures. Humans were able to exploit this by inserting themselves as “alphas.” This arrangement was relatively easy to manage as long as food and shelter were plentiful. Cats, on the other hand, are solitary hunters. They do not take direction in the same way that pack or herd animals do. How, then, did they begin cohabiting with humans? Early human settlements created a new environment for local wildlife. As villages, cities, and crop fields emerged, some animals could not adapt, while others took full advantage. Cats began hunting in fields and around grain stores and picked through trash heaps on the outskirts of settlements. Natural selection favored the cats that were able to live closest to humans and thereby gain access to more food.

In ancient Egypt, cats were more than exceptional hunters that kept pests from food; they became symbols of divinity and protection. Cats are prominent in Egyptian art, obelisks, and hieroglyphs. Egyptians worshiped cats for millennia and believed cats were magical creatures that brought good fortune to those who housed them. Egyptian mythology holds that gods and goddesses can come to Earth in the form of animals. Only the goddess Bastet, depicted as a woman with a feline head, had the power to become a cat. Cats were thought to aid in the transition to the afterlife and were sometimes buried with their owners. Wealthy families dressed their cats in jewels and fed them fancy foods. When cats died, they were mummified. As a sign of mourning, their owners would shave off their eyebrows and mourn until they grew back. Killing a cat was an offense punishable by death in ancient Egypt, even if it was an accident.

While ancient Egyptians and Romans revered cats, Europeans had a more grim view of felines. They were associated with witches and the devil. In fact, in the 13th century, an official church document called Vox in Rama was issued by Pope Gregory IX on June 13, 1233. The document declared that black cats were an incarnation of Satan. The early Christian church in Europe coexisted with witches or pagan practitioners. However, as the church gained power, witches were direct competition in gaining the hearts and minds of the people. The church began hunting, persecuting, torturing, and killing witches. Like witches, cats were difficult to control. The church did not appreciate their temperament and independence. These beliefs and perceptions led to the killing of many cats to ward off evil. Ironically, this may have contributed to the spread of the plague carried by rats across Europe.
